# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Draft.** This is an early, LLM-generated draft of the first three chapters, produced from an outline by Daniel Oberski and from extraction notes on the source literature (see `sources/extracts/` in the repository). Everything — structure, examples, exercises, claims — is provisional. The git history records what was written by the author and what was generated.
:::

This book is about a way of thinking, not a list of techniques.

Most statistics courses teach methods one at a time: here is the *t*-test, here is regression, here is ANOVA. You leave with a well-stocked toolbox and no manual — which tool answers which question, and when should anyone believe the answer? This book starts from the other end. Every empirical study, from a *t*-test to a transformer, follows the same basic logic:

> A **research question** motivates a **design** for collecting data; the design makes a set of **assumptions** plausible; those assumptions are the **model**; and the results of fitting the model answer the question — *to the extent that the assumptions hold*.

The chapters work through this logic. First the logic itself (@sec-rq-to-interpretation). Then we make it concrete: how to build a statistical model, piece by piece, out of a theory stated in words (@sec-theory-to-glm). Then its limits: some questions cannot be answered by some designs, no matter how much data you collect (@sec-identification).

Each chapter is short and contains two kinds of exercises. *Inline exercises* appear throughout; do them immediately — the answer sits right below, hidden until you click. *Test yourself* exercises at the end of each chapter are harder; they test whether you can use the ideas, not just nod along to them.

The practical exercises use R. If you prefer Python, everything here can be done there too. The ideas are what matter.
